summary: Defines conventions for using Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) algorithms, including quantum-secure ones, in the Cryptographic Message Syntax to encrypt and decrypt content. It updates RFC 5652.

eli5.summary: A KEM is a clever method for two sides to agree on a secret key. This explains how to use it to lock and unlock messages.

questions: what is a kem in cms
how does cms use post-quantum kems
subtitle: How CMS messages can be encrypted with key encapsulation mechanisms, including quantum-secure ones.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax supports key transport and key agreement for sharing the content-encryption key, but newer Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) algorithms, including quantum-secure ones, had no defined way to be used.
tldr.mechanism: A new recipient-information type, KEMRecipientInfo, carries the KEM ciphertext. A key derivation function turns the KEM shared secret into a key-encryption key, which then encrypts the content-encryption key for that recipient.
tldr.outcome: CMS enveloped-data, authenticated-data and authenticated-enveloped-data messages can now use any KEM that meets the security requirements. The RFC updates RFC 5652.

today: RFC 9629 is a Proposed Standard from August 2024 that has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 5652 by adding KEM support to CMS.

sections.title: Why CMS Needs KEMs
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) already supports key transport and key agreement to establish the key that encrypts content. RFC 5652 defines the enveloped-data content type, and RFC 5083 defines authenticated-enveloped-data. This RFC defines conventions for using Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) algorithms with these content types, and with authenticated-data.

A KEM is a one-pass (store-and-forward) mechanism for transporting random keying material to a recipient using the recipient's public key, so the originator and recipient do not have to be online at the same time. A KEM provides three functions: KeyGen() makes a key pair, Encapsulate(pk) yields a ciphertext and a shared secret for the originator, and Decapsulate(sk, ct) recovers the shared secret for the recipient.

The originator MUST implement Encapsulate(). The recipient MUST implement KeyGen() and Decapsulate(). The recipient's public key is usually carried in a certificate (RFC 5280).
sections.eli5: A KEM works like a padlock you can hand out openly. Anyone can use it to lock a secret in a box for you, but only you have the key to open it, and you do not need to be there when they lock it.

sections.title: How KEM Processing Works
sections.content:
The originator randomly generates the content-encryption key (CEK), or the content-authenticated-encryption key (CAEK). Every recipient gets that same key as an encrypted object inside the encryptedKey field of a KEMRecipientInfo. In advance, each recipient uses KeyGen() to create a key pair and makes the public key available to potential originators.

For each recipient, the originator does three things. It uses the recipient's public key with Encapsulate() to get a pairwise shared secret and a ciphertext. It uses a key derivation function (KDF) to derive a pairwise key-encryption key (KEK) from the shared secret and any data optionally sent in the ukm field. Then it uses the KEK to encrypt the CEK for that recipient. Finally the CEK encrypts the content for everyone.

The recipient reverses this: Decapsulate() with the private key and the ciphertext gives the shared secret, the KDF gives the KEK, the KEK decrypts the CEK, and the CEK decrypts the content.
sections.eli5: The sender picks one secret key for the message, then puts a copy in a separate locked parcel for each person. Each person opens their own parcel, takes out the key, and reads the message.

sections.title: The KEMRecipientInfo Structure
sections.content:
The new structure is carried in CMS as an OtherRecipientInfo, identified by the object identifier id-ori-kem, which is id-ori 3. Its fields are:

  • version: MUST be 0.
  • rid: identifies the recipient's certificate, either by issuer and serial number or by subject key identifier. The certificate MUST contain a KEM public key, and if it has a key usage extension it MUST assert the keyEncipherment bit.
  • kem: the KEM algorithm and its parameters.
  • kemct: the ciphertext from Encapsulate() for this recipient.
  • kdf: the key derivation function.
  • kekLength: the KEK size in octets, from 1 to 65535. Implementations MUST confirm it is consistent with the key-encryption algorithm in wrap.
  • ukm: optional user keying material, for example a nonce or application context. Implementations that do not support it SHOULD gracefully stop processing when it is present.
  • wrap: the key-encryption algorithm used to encrypt the CEK.
  • encryptedKey: the CEK or CAEK encrypted with the KEK.

For recipient processing, implementations MUST support both ways of specifying the certificate. For originator processing they MUST support at least one.
sections.eli5: Each parcel comes with a label saying who it is for, which kind of lock was used, and how to turn the opened lock into the key that opens the inner box.

sections.title: Deriving the Key-Encryption Key
sections.content:
The KDF takes three inputs, using the terminology of HKDF (RFC 5869). IKM is the secret input, which comes from the KEM shared secret. L is the output length in octets, taken from kekLength. info is context: the DER encoding of a CMSORIforKEMOtherInfo structure holding the wrap algorithm, the kekLength and the optional ukm. The output (OKM) is exactly L octets and is the KEK.

An acceptable KDF MUST accept an IKM, L and info. It MAY also accept a salt, carried as a parameter of the KDF algorithm identifier if present. All of these inputs MUST influence the output.

Binding the wrap algorithm and the KEK length into info ties the derived key to how it will be used.
sections.eli5: The shared secret is like a lump of clay. The key-making step shapes it into a key of exactly the right size for the lock it will be used on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The KEM MUST be designed to be secure when its public key is used many times, because the public key is expected to sit in a long-lived certificate. KEMs offering IND-CCA2 security are appropriate, and a common way to get it is the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform or a variant. The KDF, the key-encryption algorithm and the KEK SHOULD each offer at least the security level of the KEM.

KEMs do not provide data origin authentication, so with the authenticated-data content type the contents are delivered with integrity from an unknown source. Implementations MUST protect the KEM private key, the KEK and the CEK (or CAEK). Compromise of the private key may expose all content protected by it, while compromise of a KEK, CEK or CAEK may expose a single message.

The originator MUST generate a fresh KEM shared secret for each recipient and MUST discard it, along with any random value used to produce it, after building that recipient's entry. The recipient MUST discard its copy after constructing the KEK. The IKM MUST NOT be reused for any other purpose.

Effective security is set by the weaker of the key-encryption and content algorithms. The RFC's example is a 128-bit CEK for AES-CBC wrapped with AES-KEYWRAP using a 256-bit KEK: at most 128 bits of protection. Keys must come from good random numbers (see RFC 4086), and implementations should be modular so algorithms can be replaced as they weaken.
sections.eli5: A lock is only as strong as its weakest part. Every parcel must use fresh, truly random secrets that are thrown away afterwards, and the locks should be easy to swap for better ones later.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned three object identifiers. Value 3, id-ori-kem, goes in the S/MIME Other Recipient Info Identifiers registry (1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.13). Value 109, id-mod-kemAlgorithmInformation-2023, goes in the PKIX Module Identifier registry (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.0). Value 77, id-mod-cms-kemri-2023, goes in the S/MIME Module Identifier registry (1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.0).

The last two identify the two ASN.1 modules in the RFC. One defines the KEM-ALGORITHM class that describes a KEM, and the other defines KEMRecipientInfo and CMSORIforKEMOtherInfo.
sections.eli5: Official number tags were registered for the new parcel type and for the two rulebooks that describe it, so everybody uses the same labels.

messages.note: kemct from Encapsulate(); the CEK is wrapped under the KEK.

data.title: KEMRecipientInfo
data.code:
KEMRecipientInfo ::= SEQUENCE {
  version CMSVersion,  -- always set to 0
  rid RecipientIdentifier,
  kem KEMAlgorithmIdentifier,
  kemct OCTET STRING,
  kdf KeyDerivationAlgorithmIdentifier,
  kekLength INTEGER (1..65535),
  ukm [0] EXPLICIT UserKeyingMaterial OPTIONAL,
  wrap KeyEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier,
  encryptedKey EncryptedKey }
